cues.en: Hi, everyone. Thanks for coming. My name is Joel, and I don't like notebooks. So it's possible I'm the only person like this at the conference, but out in the real world, there are dozens of us, a few here. And so how did we end up here? Well, I was angry about notebooks. I tweeted that I wanted to give a talk about how I was angry about notebooks, and someone was listening, and it got accepted. And so data science luminaries thought that it sounded like an unhelpful way to spend time, and I got lots of other positive feedback about it as well.
cues.zh: 大家好，感谢光临。我叫 Joel，我不喜欢 notebook。在这个大会上，可能就我一个人是这样的，但在现实世界里，像我们这样的人可多了，这里也有几位。那我们是怎么走到这一步的呢？嗯，我当时对 notebook 很火大。我就发推说想做个演讲，讲讲我为什么讨厌 notebook，结果有人注意到了，提案还真被录用了。有些数据科学界的大佬觉得这纯粹是浪费时间，不过我也收到了很多积极正面的反馈。

cues.en: Here we are. So what kind of person not only doesn't like notebooks but goes to a conference about notebooks to talk about how he doesn't like notebooks? So I'm a research engineer at the Allen Institute for artificial intelligence. My job is Python library design and reproducible science. So I have lots of thoughts on these topics. I won't call myself a Python expert. You should never call yourself an expert. But I've been doing Python for a long time, and I have a lot of opinions about it.
cues.zh: 于是我们今天就在这儿了。那到底是什么样的人，不仅自己不喜欢 notebook，还要专门跑到 notebook 的技术大会上来大谈自己有多讨厌 notebook 呢？我是艾伦人工智能研究所的一名研发工程师。我的工作是 Python 库设计和可复现科学研究。所以对这些话题我有很多想法。我不会自称 Python 专家，人永远不该自称专家。但我写 Python 已经很久了，对此确实有很多看法。

cues.en: I was the chief data scientist at Willow Metrics. I've managed data scientists. I've mentored data scientists. I wrote a popular book on data science. So I have some thoughts about how to teach data science as well. I worked as a software engineer at Google for a couple of years. And I work on Allen NLP, which is a very well-engineered project. I make live coding videos, so I think a lot about how do I teach concepts using code.
cues.zh: 我曾是 Willow Metrics 的首席数据科学家。我管理过数据科学家，指导过数据科学家，还写过一本畅销的数据科学书。所以关于如何教授数据科学，我也有一些心得。我曾在 Google 当过几年的软件工程师。我现在参与 AllenNLP 的开发，这是一个工程化做得非常出色的项目。我还会做实时编程直播视频，所以我经常思考该如何用代码来讲解概念。

cues.en: I write a blog that's about Python sometimes, and I update it sometimes. And I co-host a data science podcast with Andrew Musman called Adversarial Learning. If you're wondering why there's no episodes recently, that's my fault. I need to edit them. Okay, so that's me. I was gonna start a timer, and I didn't, let me start now. Too fast? I have a lot of slides. Okay. Okay, so that's me. What do I assume about you? Well, you're at this conference, so possibly you think notebooks are great?
cues.zh: 我偶尔会写写关于 Python 的博客，也是随缘更新。我和 Andrew Musman 一起主持了一个名为 Adversarial Learning 的数据科学播客。如果你好奇为什么最近没更新，那是我的锅，我还没来得及剪辑。好了，这就是我。我本来打算定个计时器的，结果忘了，我现在定一个。太快了吗？因为我幻灯片实在太多了。好的。行，介绍完我了，那我是怎么看待各位的呢？既然大家都来参加这个大会了，大概率是觉得 notebook 很棒吧？

cues.en: And you came to the stocks, and maybe you want me to change your mind. And so let me just give you a couple caveats. One is that I'm not an open expert. I've tried very hard not to misrepresent notebooks, but it's possible I may have done so inadvertently. If so, I apologize. But I have a lot of complaints, so even if one is wrong, they can't all be wrong. It's also the case that I believe there are probably advanced add-ins that might address some of my concerns, but they're obscure, and I didn't know about them. And so that's why they're not here, but I apologize for not knowing about them.
cues.zh: 而你们来听这个演讲，或许是想看看我能不能改变你们的想法。那容我先打几个预防针。首先，我不是这方面的专家。我已经极力避免歪曲 notebook，但难免可能有无心之失。如果是这样，我先道个歉。不过我的槽点很多，哪怕有一条说错了，总不可能全都错吧。另外，我也相信可能存在一些高级插件能解决我的某些顾虑，但它们太冷门了，我并不知道。所以这里才没有提及，没能了解这些我也深表歉意。

cues.en: My other caveat is that there's a new product called JupyterLab. When I proposed this talk, it was not yet released. So I haven't used it very much. It's possible it addresses some of my concerns as well. It's likely it doesn't address all of them. So before I get into things I don't like about notebooks, to be fair, I want to talk about things I do like about notebooks. So one is that I really love the literate programming model. I love well-documented code. And so I like the idea of mixing markdown in code. I find this a very nice aesthetic. And it's a great way of presenting things.
cues.zh: 我还有一个提醒：有个叫 JupyterLab 的新产品。我提议这个演讲时，它还没发布。所以我用得不多。它可能也能解决我的一些担忧，但很可能不能解决全部。所以在讲我不喜欢 notebook 的地方之前，公平起见，我想先说说我喜欢 notebook 的地方。其中之一是我真的很喜欢文学编程模型。我喜欢文档完善的代码。所以我喜欢在代码里混入 markdown 的想法。我觉得这种美学很好，也是展示内容的好方式。

cues.en: Another thing I like about notebooks is that inline plots are pretty great. The story around plotting in the Python console is not a good story. And so I find this pretty nice. So those are the things I like about notebooks. Now let's get to the things that I don't like about notebooks. So this is my number one fundamental complaint, is that notebooks have tons and tons of hidden state that's easy to screw up and difficult to reason about.
cues.zh: 我喜欢 notebook 的另一点是，内联绘图相当棒。在 Python 控制台里绘图这件事可不怎么样。所以我觉得这很不错。这些就是我喜欢 notebook 的地方。现在来说我不喜欢 notebook 的地方。我的头号根本抱怨是：notebook 有大量隐藏状态，很容易搞乱，也很难推理。

cues.en: So here's some very simple Python. I define a function f, takes a number x, returns x plus 2. I set y equals f of 2. I check, is y equal 4? Yes it is, that's true. Print y, it's 4. Okay, very simple, nothing fancy going on here. Here's that same example in our notebook. Define f, x plus 2, y equals f of 2, is y 4, false. Print y, y is 5. Okay, so you're looking at that and you're thinking, you know, if you look at the numbers, those cells weren't even executed in order. So, of course it doesn't work.
cues.zh: 这里有些非常简单的 Python。我定义函数 f，接收一个数字 x，返回 x 加 2。我令 y 等于 f(2)。我检查 y 是否等于 4？是的，是真的。打印 y，是 4。好，非常简单，没什么花哨的。在 notebook 里是同样的例子。定义 f，x 加 2，y 等于 f(2)，y 是否等于 4，false。打印 y，y 是 5。你看着这个会想，看看编号就知道，这些单元格甚至都不是按顺序执行的。所以当然不对。

cues.en: OK, so let's go back and make sure that they're executed in order. Here, 1 comes before 3, comes before 4, comes before 5. But still the same result. And if you look at the numbers, it's clear that something else was run between those first two lines, which is fair. But on one hand, you have this idea that notebooks are great for iterative development. But then you also have this idea that notebooks are actually kind of dangerous unless you run each cell exactly once in order. And otherwise, you can't really rely on what the outputs of the cells are.
cues.zh: 好，那我们回去确保它们按顺序执行。这里，1 在 3 前，3 在 4 前，4 在 5 前。但结果还是一样。看编号能明显看出，前两行之间还运行了别的东西，这倒没错。但一方面，你觉得 notebook 很适合迭代开发。另一方面，你又觉得 notebook 其实有点危险，除非你严格按顺序把每个单元格只运行一次。否则，你没法真正依赖单元格的输出。

cues.en: So there's this tension there that makes me kind of uncomfortable, I guess. And some of you might be thinking that my preferred REPL also has plenty of hidden state, which it does, but that state was built up in a linear fashion just by running one command at a time. And there is history magic that I can put in a cell and see, here's all the commands that have been run. But reasoning about state is actually one of the hardest parts of coding. And so we should make it as easy as possible, not as difficult as possible.
cues.zh: 所以这里有种张力，让我有点不舒服。你们有些人可能在想，我偏好的 REPL 也有很多隐藏状态，确实如此，但那个状态是线性积累起来的，就是一次运行一条命令。我可以在单元格里用 history magic，看到所有运行过的命令。但理解状态其实是编程中最难的部分之一。所以我们应该让它尽可能简单，而不是尽可能困难。

cues.en: So here's one more. This is not photoshopped. This is not me hacking the HTML. 1, 2, 3, 4 in order. What kind of trickery is this? Well, I just edited the first cell and didn't execute it, which I did on purpose to be deceptive. But you could do that by accident, too, and really confuse yourself as well. So my next complaint is that notebooks are difficult for beginners.
cues.zh: 再来看一个例子。这不是 P 出来的，我也没去改 HTML 代码。顺序确实是 1、2、3、4。这耍的什么花招？其实我只是改了第一个单元格但没运行它，我是故意使诈的。但你也可能不小心这么干，然后把自己彻底搞懵。所以我的下一个槽点是：notebook 对新手很不友好。

cues.en: And so someone comes to you and says, I would like to learn Python. And you say, OK, that's great. Create a notebook and get going. Why do I think they're difficult for beginners? It's because these sorts of hidden state complications that I'm talking about are not obvious. So this is most people's experience of how code works. You run a line of code, you run the next line of code, it happens in order. The ability to run code snippets in arbitrary order is actually really weird if you think about it. And it's very unintuitive.
cues.zh: 有人跑来跟你说：我想学 Python。你回答：好啊，太棒了，建个 notebook 开始写吧。我为什么觉得它对新手不友好？因为我前面说的这种隐藏状态的问题，新手根本察觉不到。大多数人对代码运行的认知是这样的：跑完一行代码，再跑下一行，都是按顺序来的。仔细想想，可以按任意顺序去跑代码片段，其实非常诡异，也非常反直觉。

cues.en: And if you look at beginner tutorials, they're really either cavalier about or completely silent on this hidden state issue. So I just did a Google search and found what I could find. So this is DataQuest, Jupyter, and Omokes for Beginners, a tutorial. So they talk about some cells, and they say, this will work regardless of the order of the cells in your notebook, which addresses the issue, but not, this is dangerous. Watch out. Be careful. Don't shoot yourself in the foot.
cues.zh: 如果你去看那些新手教程，它们对这种隐藏状态的问题要么轻描淡写，要么只字不提。我就随手去 Google 搜了一下。这是 DataQuest 针对新手的 Jupyter 教程。他们讲到一些单元格时说：“无论 notebook 里单元格的顺序如何，这段代码都能跑”，这就算是提到了这个问题，但根本没警告说：“这很危险，小心点，当心搬起石头砸自己的脚。”

cues.en: And then later on, they say, most of the time, the notebook will be top to bottom. But it's common to go back and make changes. In this case, just keep an eye on the numbers and see if you have a scale output. And if your notebook is longer than a page, or you can't hold 30 numbers in your head like that, then not sure. So this is Jupyter Notebook Tutorial, the definitive guide. It did not have anything about order for state. It was just stated differently. Hidden, nothing. Sequence, nothing.
cues.zh: 接着后面又说：“大多数情况下 notebook 是从上往下跑的，但回头去改代码也很常见。遇到这种情况，多留心单元格编号，看看输出是不是过时了。”可要是你的 notebook 超过一页，或者你脑子里记不住那么三四十个数字编号，那该怎么办？这篇叫《Jupyter Notebook 终极指南》，里面完全没提状态顺序的问题。我换了各种词搜，“隐藏”搜不到，“时序”搜不到，

cues.en: enough rope to hang yourself, nothing. So it didn't seem to mention the issue. Here was the comprehensive beginner's guide to Jupyter notebooks for data science and machine learning. It also did not seem to address the issue. So back to this example where I skipped cell two. You people are all notebook experts, and so the problem here is kind of obvious to you. And also, this is a really simple example. It couldn't be much simpler than this.
cues.zh: “作茧自缚”也搜不到，看来是压根没提这档子事。还有这篇《数据科学与机器学习的 Jupyter Notebook 新手全攻略》，似乎也完全回避了这个问题。回到我跳过第二个单元格的那个例子。在座的各位都是 notebook 老手了，一眼就能看出问题所在。况且那只是个极其简单的例子，简单得不能再简单了。

cues.en: For beginners who have dozens of cells and more complex code, this is utterly confusing. And I know this because they come to me with their problems. In fact, the original angry tweet that launched this talk was a result of me helping someone who was new to Python and came to me and said, Python makes no sense. I don't understand it. It doesn't behave the way a programming language should. And what happened was Python worked exactly the way they expected it to, but they'd been very loose with
cues.zh: 但对那些写了几十个单元格、代码更复杂的新手来说，这完全能把人搞疯。我之所以知道，是因为他们老跑来找我求助。实际上，催生这场演讲的那条愤怒推文，就是因为我当时在帮一个刚学 Python 的人。他跑来跟我抱怨说：“Python 简直不可理喻，我完全搞不懂，它根本就不像一门编程语言该有的样子。”事实是 Python 的运行机制完全符合预期，但他自己在 notebook 里胡乱

cues.en: stayed in execution out of order in the notebooks and ended up in a situation that appeared to make no sense. And this has happened to me multiple times. And you might be thinking, lots of beginners use notebooks, so clearly it can't be that difficult. And it's not that it's insurmountably difficult. It's that the out of order execution makes learning Python more confusing than it needs to be. OK, so my next complaint is that notebooks encourage bad habits. So you've got folders full of these. I've got folders full of these.
cues.zh: 乱改状态、乱序执行，最终陷入了一种看似毫无逻辑的死胡同。这种事我碰到过好多次。你可能会想：那么多新手都在用 notebook，显然没那么难吧。确实不是说难到无法克服，而是这种乱序执行会让学 Python 变得多此一举地混乱。好了，我的下一个槽点是：notebook 会助长坏习惯。你们的文件夹里肯定堆满了这种东西，我自己的文件夹里也是。

cues.en: Everyone's got folders full of these. So there's this sense in the data science community, which I find super unfortunate, which is that data science code doesn't need to follow the rules of good software engineering. And this was posed as a great tip, although apparently this was a misrepresentation of the tip, which I didn't learn until after I started a big Twitter fight over it.
cues.zh: 每个人都有装满这些的文件夹。所以数据科学界有一种观念，我觉得非常不幸，就是数据科学代码不需要遵循良好软件工程的规则。这曾被当作一个很棒的技巧提出来，虽然显然这曲解了那个技巧；我是直到在 Twitter 上为此大吵一架之后才知道的。

cues.en: But if you take one thing away from my talk, it should be nothing to do with notebooks. It should be that data science code should follow the rules of good software engineering. And sometimes people will say, I don't need to be rigorous about my engineering because I'm just experimenting. OK, well, experimenting is doing science. And to say, I don't need to be rigorous because I'm doing science doesn't make much sense to me. Sometimes people will say, I just want to see if my model works before I put it in production. Well,
cues.zh: 但如果我的演讲只能让你记住一件事，那不该和 Notebook 有关。而应该是：数据科学代码应该遵循良好软件工程的规则。有时人们会说，我不需要对工程严谨，因为我只是在做实验。好吧，实验就是在做科学。说“我在做科学，所以不需要严谨”，这在我听来不太说得通。有时人们会说，我只想在把模型上生产之前看看它能不能工作。那么，

cues.en: And if you want to find out if it works, you need to write it correctly and make sure that your code is correct. So another line of thought here is that people will say, I need to write my code as fast as possible. And doing poor software engineering allows me to write my code as fast as possible. I don't agree that that's even true, but generally speaking,
cues.zh: 而如果你想知道它能不能工作，你就得把它写对，并确保代码是正确的。所以这里还有另一种想法：人们会说，我需要尽可能快地写代码。而糟糕的软件工程能让我尽可能快地写代码。我甚至不认为这是真的，但一般来说，

cues.en: Trying to write your code as fast as possible is great if you're doing a live coding presentation, perhaps. But it's not great when you're trying to do reproducible science and rigorous work. So having taken a broad tour of the Jupyter ecosystem, a really unfair cynical take is that a lot of things that people build are to allow people not to have to develop good habits.
cues.zh: 如果你是在做现场编码演示，也许尽可能快地写代码很棒。但当你想做可复现的科学和严谨的工作时，这就不棒了。所以在广泛浏览了 Jupyter 生态之后，一个非常不公平且刻薄的看法是：人们构建的很多东西，是为了让人不必养成好习惯。

cues.en: You don't want to develop good habits with this for you. So this is just a blog post that came across my radar. I think I probably saw it on Twitter. It's just some random blog post, but Paco liked it, so there must be something to it. It's how to present your data science results in a Jupyter Notebook the right way. And then it says, how to import one Jupyter Notebook into another. OK, so here's someone who wrote some code, some function, and doesn't want their client or decision maker to see it.
cues.zh: 你不想靠这个养成好习惯。所以，这只是我偶然看到的一篇博客文章。我想我可能是在 Twitter 上看到的。它只是一篇随便的博客文章，但 Paco 喜欢它，所以它肯定有点东西。文章讲的是如何以正确的方式在 Jupyter Notebook 中展示你的数据科学结果。然后它又说，如何把一个 Jupyter Notebook 导入另一个。好，所以这里有个人写了一些代码、某个函数，却不想让客户或决策者看到它。

cues.en: So they've invented a couple kinds of magic that allow this to happen. So it turns out, here's some code I wrote, but I don't want my client to see. It's actually a solved problem that people who do Python know how to do. But if you insist on putting everything in a notebook, then it's not a solved problem without this kind of thing. And in the comments, people actually pointed this out to the author and said, you should really just write modules and libraries and test them and be clean.
cues.zh: 所以他们发明了几种魔法来实现这一点。结果就是，这是我写的一些代码，但我不想让客户看到。其实这是一个已解决的问题，写 Python 的人知道该怎么做。但如果你坚持把所有东西都放进 Notebook，那没有这类东西的话，这就不是一个已解决的问题。而且在评论里，人们确实向作者指出了这一点，说：你真的应该直接写模块和库，测试它们，保持整洁。

cues.en: And the author kind of admitted, I agree, that would be better than what I proposed here. But this takes into account that data scientists write bad code. And yes, this is hard to debug, I agree with you. But anyway, but this blog post was called The Right Way. OK, so notebooks encourage bad habits. They also discourage good habits. So here is some code from a live coding demonstration I do about building a deep learning library. On the left, you can see that I've nicely segregated things into
cues.zh: 作者也算承认了，说我同意，那确实比我这里提的做法更好。但这考虑到了数据科学家写代码很烂的情况。确实，这很难调试，我同意你的看法。但不管怎样，这篇博文的名字可叫作《正确之道》。好吧，Notebook 会助长坏习惯，同时也会抑制好习惯。这里是我在一场构建深度学习库的现场编码演示中的一些代码。在左边，你可以看到我把内容清晰地拆分成了

cues.en: There's a loss module. There's an optimizer's module. There's a tensor module. And on the right-hand side, you can see that I've used classes and inheritance. And I've made this code so that it's very clean and testable and reusable. And this is something that I live code in an hour. So it's hard for me to accept that it's too slow to do things this way. So how do we make sure our code works? We write tests for it.
cues.zh: 一个损失函数模块，一个优化器模块，还有一个张量模块。而在右侧，你可以看到我使用了类和继承。我把代码写得非常整洁、易测试且可复用。而这是我在一小时内现场手敲出来的。所以我很难接受“用这种方式写代码太慢了”的说法。那我们怎么保证代码能正常工作呢？写测试。

cues.en: how to make sure it keeps working after we make changes to it. We run those tests. Is it important that we use that kind of discipline when we're writing code to do science? Of course it is. And notebooks don't easily lend themselves to the kind of rigorous unit testing that you can get when you write things in terms of libraries, which does not say that it's impossible to do, but it's not natural to do. Here's how I write code.
cues.zh: 怎么保证改完代码后它依然正常？运行那些测试。在写科学计算代码时，保持这种规范重要吗？当然重要。而 Notebook 很难自然地支持那种写成库形式时能获得的严格单元测试，这倒不是说完全做不到，但确实不够自然。下面是我写代码的方式。

cues.en: I use lots of type hints, and I run MyPity to type check them. You probably don't write code this way, in part because I haven't lectured you about it enough.
